Nov 26 : US tobacco group Altria said on Thursday it was considering a possible all-cash offer for Imperial Brands and was in talks with another party over part of the British company's business, as Japan Tobacco also was reported to be weighing a bid. Shares in London-listed Imperial Brands soared as much as 17.6 per cent to 3,562 pence, giving it a market capitalisation of £26.77 billion ($35.07 billion). Bloomberg News earlier on Thursday reported that Japan Tobacco is evaluating a potential acquisition of Imperial Brands, citing people familiar with the matter. Last week, Imperial Brands, which makes Winston cigarettes, announced plans to cut up to 4,600 jobs, or nearly a fifth of its workforce as it tightens its grip on costs amid falling cigarette volumes and rising competition.

Imperial's brands also include Davidoff, Gauloises, West and Kool menthol cigarettes, as well as Rizla rolling papers. Japan Tobacco's portfolio includes Camel and Benson & Hedges. Altria's family of companies includes Philip Morris USA — the maker of Marlboro in the United States. Altria said it was also in discussions with a third party for a part of Imperial Brands' business, although no agreement had yet been reached. The Japanese group has been speaking with advisers as it weighs a possible transaction, the report said, adding that JT has considered teaming up with a partner to buy Imperial and then split up the British company's assets in different parts of the world. Imperial Brands declined to comment and Japan Tobacco did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A deal for Imperial Brands would rank among the largest recent acquisitions of a British company by an overseas buyer. ($1 = 0.7634 pounds)

Source: Reuters

FAST

BRUSSELS, Nov 26 : Chinese e-commerce platform Temu has committed to bringing several of its commercial practices in line with EU consumer protection laws, the European Commission said on Thursday. "Temu's commitments concern a broad range of commercial practices that mislead consumers or unduly influence their purchasing decisions, including fake discounts, fake reviews, pressure selling, forced gamification, and missing and misleading information," the Commission said in a statement. Temu, which is owned by PDD Holdings, said it would provide clearer and more accessible information for customer support, prices, environmental claims and checkout, and would make refunds easier. Temu also committed to ending forced gamification features, like spinning the wheel to access the marketplace, and pressure-selling messages, the Commission said. A Temu spokesperson said the company was pleased to have reached a resolution. "We appreciate the constructive engagement throughout the process and will continue to strengthen transparency and improve the shopping experience for consumers across Europe." Countries will now monitor Temu's compliance with its commitments. Failing to comply could lead to fines of 4 per cent or more of Temu's annual turnover in the concerned member states.

Source: Reuters

PARIS, Nov 26 : FIFA said on Thursday it had been the victim of a criminal cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information. A person with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters that no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed. "FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information," a FIFA spokesperson told Reuters. FIFA strongly condemned the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data, adding that such actions were "a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy".

Its reference to publication did not say whether any data had appeared online, or where. FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in July that his organisation had scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors following a widespread backlash. FAST

AMSTERDAM, Nov 26 : Dutch consumer and digital rights groups asked a court on Thursday to halt sales of Meta AI-powered smart glasses in the Netherlands, arguing they violate European privacy laws by allowing wearers to film people without their knowledge. While limited in scope to the Netherlands, a summary ruling in the civil suit against Meta at the Amsterdam District Court could set a precedent amid growing public backlash, venue bans and regulatory warnings across the world. The groups, which include the Netherlands' main consumer association Consumentenbond and Offlimits, which campaigns against online sex abuse, argued that the glasses developed by Meta and Ray-Ban owner EssilorLuxottica both violate privacy laws and force people to constantly worry in public places, with a chilling effect on society. The plaintiffs want Meta to prevent its glasses from being used to record people without their knowledge, stop using recordings to train AI models and halt sales until Meta complies. They sought penalties of €100,000 ($109,600) per day per defendant for non-compliance, capped at €100 million.

Offlimits' lawyer Karlijn Han said the glasses were used for what she described in court as "creep shots." "Covert recordings are undoubtedly also being made during exams, in changing rooms, at swimming pools, in hotel rooms and hospitals, but also in playgrounds and on beaches," she said in opening remarks. "Each invasion of privacy is worse than the last." META DENIES IMAGES ARE USED TO TRAIN AI Meta's lawyer Bastiaan Kemp said the court should reject the suit. He said the measures demanded would harm legitimate users, damage Meta's competitive position and amount to a product recall without resolving concerns about similar devices. “Providers of products cannot be held responsible for every instance of deliberate misuse,” he told the court. He said that a recording light on the frame makes it obvious when they are being used for recording. And he denied allegations made by Consumentenbond's lawyer in court that Meta processes images recorded by the smart glasses in Europe or uses them to train AI models in violation of European law. Meta and manufacturing partner EssilorLuxottica sold more than 7 million smart glasses in 2025, around 80 per cent of the global market. A lawyer for EssilorLuxottica argued that it neither processes nor has access to footage and that a sales ban would be disproportionate and ineffective given the availability of similar products from other manufacturers. BACKLASH EXTENDS WORLDWIDE From proposed restrictions in Australia and Norway to bans in courts across England, Wales and New York state, governments and judicial authorities are increasingly seeking to prevent covert recording and protect sensitive information. Cinema operators in the UK are also introducing restrictions over privacy and film piracy concerns.   On Tuesday, Germany's national consumer federation announced legal action against Meta and Ray-Ban over alleged privacy violations, arguing that the glasses make it nearly impossible for consumers to comply with European data protection rules when using them in public. The European Data Protection Board warned in October that smart glasses raised serious privacy concerns and called for stronger safeguards. Dutch privacy regulator AP this month advised consumers to not buy smart glasses, saying they are unsafe for both users and bystanders. In October, Dutch retail chain Hans Anders suspended sales of Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses in the Netherlands and Belgium. Meta also faces proposed class-action lawsuits in the United States over alleged improper sharing of private images gathered by the glasses. A date for a decision in the Dutch case has not yet been set but is expected in mid-December. ($1 = 0.9124 euros)

Source: Reuters

HONG KONG, Nov 26 : Standard Chartered's cryptocurrency custody unit Zodia Custody suffered a security breach earlier this week that exposed some client and employee information, the unit's chief executive told Reuters on Thursday. The breach, detected by Zodia on Monday, resulted in some client and staff data, including names and email addresses, being leaked, Zodia Custody CEO Richard Clark said in an emailed statement. The company's London-listed shares were up 2.6 per cent on the day. "Based on our investigation to date, there have been no unauthorised transactions," Clark said.

The incident is a setback for the Asia- and Africa-focused lender's digital asset ambitions, coming weeks after it increased its stake in Zodia to 100 per cent as it expands its cryptocurrency business amid growing mainstream adoption of digital assets. Zodia on Monday took offline software that allows institutional clients' systems to connect directly to its platform after detecting what Clark described as attempts to probe its systems. The service has since been restored, and affected clients and regulators have been notified, he added. On Tuesday, Zodia determined that an unauthorised party had accessed "limited" client information, including organisation details and, for a small number of clients and employees, a business contact name and email address, Clark said. The breach adds to a growing list of cybersecurity incidents affecting financial institutions as hackers deploy increasingly sophisticated tools, although it is not clear whether artificial intelligence played any role in this case.

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia will require AirAsia to give it priority over other lenders if the government agrees to provide support to the budget airline, the country's finance minister said on Thursday (Nov 26). Officials have said they are assessing ways to provide support without risking public funds. Authorities are monitoring AirAsia's financial health as airlines around the world grapple with a jump in jet fuel prices linked to the Iran war. AirAsia has said it was aiming to raise up to US$1 billion from international debt markets as well as 700 million ringgit in local credit facilities, with the fundraising expected to be completed between December and February. Shares in the airline, which controls about 60 per cent of Malaysia's domestic aviation market and employs about 26,000 people, have lost about 72 per cent of their value this year. AirAsia posted a narrower loss in the third quarter, but warned of rising fuel costs as it works to boost liquidity.

LONDON, Nov 26 : Crude oil prices edged up on Thursday, reversing earlier losses, after Yemen's Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery and Iran said mines struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz, reviving concerns about supply disruption. Brent crude futures were up 35 cents, or 0.37 per cent, at $94.96 a barrel at 1211 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 76 cents, or 0.91 per cent, to $84.44 a barrel. There will be no settlement for WTI on Thursday because of the US Thanksgiving holiday.  "The perceived supply surplus in the coming months and quarters and sticky inflation, which forces central banks to raise rates, resulting in a stronger dollar, will possibly set a ceiling on any attempt to push prices significantly higher," said PVM Oil Associates analyst Tamas Varga.

The refinery, Saudi Arabia's largest, is part of a complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude, and analysts expect the latest reported Houthi attacks to increase oil's geopolitical risk premium. The Saudi government and state oil firm Aramco did not immediately respond to requests for comment.  At the same time, shipping has been disrupted through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil supply had been recovering to near pre-war levels.  Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday that two tankers had exploded and caught fire after hitting sea mines north of Oman's Khasab port while attempting to cross the Strait. One of the vessels was a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, the Guards said.  "The broadening of the Middle East conflict threatens to halt the recovery in oil flows in recent weeks," said ANZ analyst Daniel Hynes. They face the challenge of balancing output with the United Arab Emirates no longer in the group, and with Iraq and Kazakhstan pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their oil production capacity. Two people with knowledge of the matter said OPEC+ may roll over its current oil output targets at the upcoming meeting. In the US, crude stocks rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, the Energy Information Administration said, also supporting prices as analysts had expected a 1.5 million-barrel rise. In Asia, Thailand's Bangchak Corp said it had shut all production units at its Phra Khanong oil refinery in Bangkok following a fire.

FAST

NEW DELHI, Nov 26 : India's main opposition Congress party has sued Meta and the federal government, saying that an automated content-removal system is blocking political posts and images of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi ahead of state elections.   The filing takes a week-long Congress campaign against Meta from the streets to the courtroom, and highlights Prime Minister Narendra Modi's automated takedown mandate, under which the Facebook and Instagram parent has restricted more than 5.4 million posts in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in all of 2025.  In a court filing dated November 25 in the Delhi High Court, seen by Reuters, Congress' youth wing social media head Manu Jain said the rules have become "an instrument for the suppression of lawful political expression". The case leaves Meta's operations in India, the company's biggest market, caught between a government whose rules strip platforms of legal protection if they fail to comply, and an opposition demanding it push back.

Congress argues that Meta's system is blocking posts that are not "exactly identical" copies of content previously ordered removed, including birthday greetings, tributes and a wedding invitation featuring Gandhi. Meta says it moderates content in India in accordance with the law. Meta declined to comment. India's IT and home ministries, which are named as co-respondents in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Modi's government has maintained that such laws are essential to prevent the proliferation of illegal and harmful content online in a market of over 1.1 billion internet users. Congress is urging the court to strike down the mandate for automated takedowns and also order Meta to restore the posts, as well as disclose blocking criteria. Hearings are expected to begin in the coming days. "AUTOMATED TOOLS" MANDATE India amended its IT rules in February to require large platforms to use technical measures "including automated tools" to find and block any post "exactly identical" to content already removed under a court order or a written government notice. Before that, platforms were asked only to "endeavour" to use such tools. To comply, Meta has been restricting "100 per cent identical copies of content, at scale and in country" under India's amended IT rules, its transparency report shows. The company says it is still testing and refining the system given the "unprecedented nature of this effort". Meta says it is required to automatically restrict content at scale in only a "limited" number of countries, which it says explains the higher volumes. Congress says the automated system is catching far more than exact duplicates. It is blocking birthday greetings, tributes and even a wedding invitation because they carry the photograph or name of opposition leader Gandhi, while "no order, notice, reason or even a 'legal request' has been disclosed," the petition said. In one case cited in the petition, a November 8 birthday greeting from a youth wing leader to a colleague, showing the colleague standing beside Gandhi, was blocked the same day. "We restricted access to this content through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements," the notice to the user read.  India is also one of seven markets, including Brazil and Hong Kong, where Meta does not tell users which government authority sought a restriction, citing "legal obligations and regulatory considerations", its transparency report shows. Elsewhere, it does so in most cases. WIDER OFFENSIVE BY CONGRESS   The automated takedown system "distorts the level playing field" needed for a free and fair election, especially as party workers rely on Meta's platforms to reach voters ahead of state polls due early next year, the petition says. Facebook and Instagram have 400 million and 515 million users respectively in India, according to research firm DataReportal. Congress has put up large hoardings in several cities depicting Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg in the traditional uniform of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the ideological parent of Modi's party. Congress' youth wing has protested near Meta offices and clashed with police in several cities in recent days. The BJP has accused the protesters of vandalising the offices of private companies. At a closed-door meeting this week reported by Reuters, Congress told Meta to push back against first-instance takedown orders, as Elon Musk's X has done, a source told Reuters. X is currently engaged in a legal battle against the government over its content-removal system. Meta told Congress at the meeting that it is neutral towards all political parties and bound by local laws.

Source: Reuters

TOKYO, Nov 26 : The Bank of Japan's net income shrank in the first half of the fiscal year that ends in March 2027, as rising interest rates boosted payments made on excess reserves parked with the central bank, its earnings data showed on Thursday. While dividends from its holdings of exchange-traded funds offset some of the higher interest costs, the data highlights the strain the BOJ's rate hikes are inflicting on its balance sheet. Since exiting a decade-long, massive stimulus programme in 2024, the BOJ has raised its short-term policy rate several times, including in September. The rate now stands at 1.25 per cent. The BOJ pays the same 1.25 per cent interest rate on the excess reserves that financial institutions park with the central bank under a programme aimed at controlling money market rates around its policy rate.

Overall, the BOJ's net income fell to 1.55 trillion yen from 1.71 trillion yen a year earlier. The BOJ pays most of the net income earned each year to the government, which uses it to fund spending. S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade on Wednesday (Nov 25), saying the departure and subsequent reinstatement of its CEO had exposed weaknesses in the chipmaker's management and board oversight . "We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence. The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler," the ratings agency said. The move comes amid a turbulent period for Nvidia's leadership. The company's board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang earlier this week, days after he resigned following revelations of extramarital affairs with his direct reports as well as a Chinese businesswoman alleged by US intelligence to be Beijing's spy . Critics and lawmakers slammed the reinstatement, questioning the independence of the board, whose newly elected chair had told investors last week Nvidia would not rehire Huang as CEO because his personal behaviour was inconsistent with the company's code of conduct.

Instead, it concluded that there was no evidence he had broken any laws based on ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro and Megaspeed International , which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China. The agency said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects. Meanwhile, Moody's said on Wednesday that bringing back Huang eases near-term uncertainty around Nvidia's business execution and eliminates execution risk associated with appointing a new leader for the chipmaker. Elon Musk, the world's richest person, said on Wednesday (Nov 25) that every child in the US will receive two shares in SpaceX, the space and AI company he runs, pledging a gift worth some US$18 billion. Musk and rival AI company Anthropic have recently laid out sharply different blueprints for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom, amid growing public and political scrutiny of the industry. Children will receive one share from the company and one from him personally, Musk said in a brief post on X, without providing details. In a separate post, Musk said the SpaceX shares will be transferred next month.

"The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," Musk added. SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk will personally match the number of shares donated by the company. A Trump Account is a program designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at US$127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly US$18 billion.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Musk's SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts. "What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base," said Christopher Brankin, global markets advisor at brokerage Mitrade Group. "It builds immediate market engagement and creates a massive, financially literate client pipeline for trading platforms as that generation comes of age." Musk, whose net worth is around US$824 billion, said last month he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June. "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X at the time. "Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way," Musk added. Most of Musk's philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than US$14 billion in assets.

In October, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump initiative. Anthropic, which recently went public, said last month it was committing 5 per cent of its shares to a new fund for the "public good". It said that the initiative, worth around US$54 billion at current prices, will give it more flexibility and scale to make donations for the benefit of humanity. Other executives have also set up major, long-running philanthropy ventures. Berkshire Hathaway Chairman Emeritus Warren Buffett, one of the most prominent figures in philanthropy, is reported to have given away US$60 billion so far, with most of the rest of his roughly US$150 billion fortune slated for philanthropy too. The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has distributed more than US$100 billion since its founding in 2000, with some of that fueled by donations from Buffett.

FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 26 : Australian business investment surged anew in the September quarter as firms poured money into data centres, recording its biggest rise since 2011 at the height of the mining boom, while companies further upgraded spending plans for coming months. The strong numbers on Thursday suggested some resilience in the Australian economy even as five interest rate hikes this year triggered the biggest housing downturn in 40 years, hit consumer spending and weakened the labour market. The local dollar rose 0.2 per cent to $0.6640 and three-year government bond futures reversed earlier gains to be down three ticks to 95.51. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported private capital spending jumped 12.2 per cent in the third quarter to an inflation-adjusted A$59.5 billion ($39.37 billion), far above market forecasts of a 4.4 per cent rise.  That was led by an 87 per cent jump in spending on information media and telecommunications equipment amid record investment in server racks and processing gear for data centres. Much of this was on imported equipment and thus an offsetting drag on economic growth.

Abhijit Surya, senior APAC economist at Capital Economics, said spending on information and communications technology could nearly double in the 2027 financial year, in contrast with the rest of the economy, where capital spending was struggling to tread water. "With the RBA clearly concerned about capacity pressures, the data suggest it won’t be in a rush to cut rates anytime soon," Surya said.  Markets are still wagering that the next move in interest rates will be down, but do not fully price a first cut from the Reserve Bank of Australia until August. A June cut is now seen as an 83 per cent chance. Overall spending on plant and machinery shot up 23.1 per cent, while spending on buildings and structures rose 1.7 per cent. An ABS survey of firms showed they planned to spend A$223.7 billion in the year to June 2027, 11.8 per cent higher than the previous estimate. ($1 = 1.5113 Australian dollars)

Source: Reuters
